notes.meaning: Sarai had not been able to have children, even though God had promised Abram a large family. Years earlier, the family had stayed in Egypt, where they likely acquired Hagar as a servant girl. Sarai carried the deep sorrow of being barren as the years passed by.

Sarai knew that God controlled the womb, but she grew impatient and tried to solve the problem by herself. By local custom, a wife could give her personal slave to her husband so that any child born would count as the wife's own. Abram agreed to Sarai's plan instead of asking God what to do.

differ.view: Many Reformed teachers see Abram listening to Sarai as a parallel to Adam listening to Eve, viewing this as a spiritual fall in Abram's life.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Ancient Near Eastern legal records show that giving a female servant as a surrogate wife was an accepted legal practice for childless couples of that time.

notes.meaning: Abram and Sarai had lived in Canaan for ten full years, and the long delay sorely tested their faith. Sarai gave Hagar to Abram to be a secondary wife so they could produce a child. Taking another wife went against God's original design for marriage to be between one man and one woman.

Hagar conceived quickly, proving that Abram was able to father children. Once Hagar realized she was pregnant, she became proud and began to look down on Sarai. What seemed like a clever human plan immediately brought jealousy and disrespect into the household.

Sarai became furious over the contempt she received and blamed Abram for the trouble. She felt her husband was failing to protect her dignity and keep the servant in her place. In her anger, she rashly demanded that the Lord step in and judge between them.

Abram wanted to keep peace in his home, so he handed authority over Hagar back to Sarai. Sarai then treated her maidservant so harshly that Hagar ran away into the desert. Running away left the young mother-to-be alone, frightened, and without protection.

The angel of the Lord found Hagar resting by a spring along the desert road leading to Shur, which went toward Egypt. This showed that God cares for those who are helpless and forgotten. Many Christian teachers see this special angel as an appearance of God the Son before He came to earth as Jesus.

The angel addressed her as Sarai's maidservant, reminding her who she was and what duties she had left behind. He asked where she had come from and where she was going, inviting her to speak honestly. Hagar admitted that she was simply running away from her mistress's harsh treatment.

The angel gave Hagar the difficult command to return to Sarai and submit to her authority. God called her to choose obedience and humility rather than escaping into the desert. Returning to Abram's home was also the only safe place for her unborn child.

The angel gave Hagar a wonderful promise to encourage her to obey. He declared that her future family line would grow so large that nobody would be able to count them. Because the angel spoke with divine authority to multiply her offspring, he spoke as God Himself.

The angel announced that she would bear a son and instructed her to name him Ishmael, which means "God hears." This is the first time in the Bible that a baby was named by God before being born. The boy's name would be a lifelong reminder that the Lord had listened to Hagar in her misery.

God revealed that Ishmael would be like a wild desert donkey, loving independence and refusing to be tamed. He and his descendants would live in constant friction with their neighbors and survive through strength. God promised to protect and grow his family, though Ishmael would not be the heir of the covenant promise.

Hagar was filled with wonder that the living God knew all about a runaway Egyptian slave. She praised the Lord as "the God who sees me" because He watched over her in her darkest hour. She was also amazed that she had caught a glimpse of God and survived.

Because of this encounter, the spring in the wilderness between Kadesh and Bered was named Beer-lahai-roi. That name means "the well of the Living One who sees me." The spring remained a lasting monument to God's mercy toward someone in deep despair.

Hagar followed God's direction, returned to Abram's tents, and gave birth to her baby boy. Abram gave the child the name Ishmael, showing that he believed Hagar's story and respected the angel's instruction. Abram publicly honored the promise that God had heard Hagar's cries.

Abram was eighty-six years old when Ishmael was born into his family. It had been eleven years since he first set out from Haran following God's call. He would still need to wait another fourteen years before Isaac, the child promised through Sarai, would arrive.
